extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and Roman history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarises the factors Lecky uses to assess the moral state of the Roman Empire — social, economic, cultural, and institutional indicators that signal moral decline or vitality. Useful for applying these criteria to historical or comparative moral analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of corrupt and corrupting professions
rubrics_metrics.description: The immense increase of corrupt and corrupting professions, as actors, pantomimes, hired gladiators, political spies, ministers to passion, astrologers, religious charlatans, pseudo-philosophers, which gave the free classes a precarious and occasional subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These professions supplied the idle with precarious livelihoods and contributed to moral degradation by orienting popular life toward sensation, flattery, and vice rather than productive or civic pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of clientage and parasitism
rubrics_metrics.description: Every rich man was surrounded by a train of dependants, who lived in a great measure at his expense, and spent their lives in ministering to his passions and flattering his vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clientage created widespread servility and dependency, hollowing out public spirit and honorable channels of ambition while fostering corruption and sycophancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public distribution of corn and money (bread and circuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public distribution of corn, and occasionally of money, was carried on to such an extent, that, so far as the first necessaries of life were concerned, the whole poor free population of Rome was supported gratuitously by the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lavish and untargeted distributions produced absolute idleness, a sense of entitlement (received as a right), and undermined productive enterprise and civic responsibility — a principal imperial policy with deeply corrosive consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratuitous public amusements (games, baths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratuitous public amusements still further diverted them from labour; the attractions of the games, and especially of the public baths, which became the habitual resort of the idle, combined with the charms of the Italian climate ... to draw the poor citizens from indoor life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public spectacles and leisure institutions acted as powerful diversions from work and civic participation, reinforcing habits of idleness and sensuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic decay: celibacy, abortion, infanticide, and exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: The population rapidly dwindled away ... the general practice of abortion among the rich, and of infanticide and exposition in all classes, still further checked the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread practices that reduced birthrates and family continuity are presented as both symptoms and causes of social and moral decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of public spirit / indifference to liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Empire all liberty was cheerfully bartered for games and corn ... the Roman now, as then, asks only for an idle subsistence and for public spectacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A populace that prefers immediate comforts and spectacles to liberty and civic responsibility indicates profound moral erosion; historical examples (people plundering houses, cheering armies) illustrate this indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of rival powers to reanimate civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: An empire which comprised all the civilised globe could know nothing of this political interaction ... the enslaved provinces could have no influence in rekindling political life in the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky treats the lack of independent, rival nations as a structural cause of civic stagnation — without external examples or competition, patriotism and liberty atrophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decay of agriculture and loss of peasant proprietors
rubrics_metrics.description: Productive enterprise was almost extinct in Italy ... The peasant proprietor soon glided hopelessly into debt. The immense advantages which slavery gave the rich gradually threw nearly all the Italian soil into their hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration of land, slave labour, importation of grain, and abandonment of cultivation destroyed rural virtues and the social habits cultivated by peasant proprietorship; numerous attempted remedies failed against these structural forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military deterioration: recruitment, discipline, and loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roman army was at first recruited exclusively from the upper classes ... Military pay, foreign mercenaries, abolition of property qualifications, removal of legions from Italy, and transfer of allegiance from sovereign to general all undermined discipline and patriotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in recruitment, indemnification, long foreign stations, and soldiers' political power produced insubordination and a tendency for armies to elect emperors, contributing to military anarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits of inactivity incompatible with military service
rubrics_metrics.description: The habits of inactivity which the Imperial policy had produced ... led to a profound disinclination for the hardships of military life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread civilian idleness eroded the cultural and physical habits necessary for effective military service, accelerating military decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gladiatorial games as a central sign of moral atrocity
rubrics_metrics.description: The gladiatorial games form ... the one feature of Roman society which to a modern mind is almost inconceivable in its atrocity ... originally religious ceremonies celebrated at the tombs of the great, and intended as human sacrifices to appease the Manes of the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky treats the games as both symptom and cause of moral degradation: religious origins, political uses, imperial expansion, and the spectacle's scale (Colosseum, Titus, Trajan) are used to show how normalized brutality became integral to public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erosion of refined taste and dramatic art by spectacle of blood
rubrics_metrics.description: To those who were habituated to the intense realism of the amphitheatre, the idealised suffering of the stage was unimpressive ... The gladiatorial games ... destroyed all sense of disgust, and therefore all refinement of taste, and they rendered the permanent triumph of the drama impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By removing natural disgust at suffering, the games undermined the theatre's moral function (cultivating compassion and refined taste), diminishing the cultural conditions for tragic art and humane sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desensitization to human (and animal) suffering; pleasure in suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: When men have regarded it as not a crime to kill some class of their fellow-men, they have soon learnt to do so with no more natural compunction ... there is scarcely a human being who might not by custom be so indurated as to share it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated exposure produces indifference or even aesthetic pleasure in suffering (examples: Claudius enjoying dying countenances; spectators signalling life or death with thumbs), indicating deep moral corrosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craving for novelty driving refinements of barbarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere desire for novelty impelled the people to every excess or refinement of barbarity ... bears and bulls chained together, criminals thrown to maddened beasts, enormous numbers of animals and men killed in single days or festivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appetite for ever-intensified spectacles led to escalating cruelty and inventiveness in methods of killing; numerical and exotic spectacle (elephants, crocodiles, vast combats) exemplify this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cultural justifications that normalize brutality
rubrics_metrics.description: The games ... were afterwards defended as a means of sustaining the military spirit ... argued that the death of the gladiator was both more honourable and more merciful than that of the passive victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious tradition, notions of military training, punishment of criminals, and perceived honour provided moral cover for brutality, preventing broader condemnation and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited moral protest and weakness of opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely few of the moralists of the Roman Empire ever advanced (a full condemnation) ... Seneca denounced the shows; Plutarch condemned combats of wild beasts; Marcus Aurelius limited harm — but such protests were rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scarcity and limited success of moral protests against spectacles and cruelty illustrate how deeply the practices were entrenched and socially accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative provincial prosperity under imperial administration
rubrics_metrics.description: As far as the distant provinces were concerned, it is probable that the Imperial system was on the whole a good. Ample municipal freedom, good roads, and for the most part wise and temperate rulers, secured for the distant sections of the empire a large measure of prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky signals a contrast: while Italy decayed morally and economically, many provinces benefited from imperial order — this duality serves as a criterion to judge different regional moral/economic outcomes under the same polity.
